title: When Can You Poison Rewards? A Tight Characterization of Reward Poisoning in Linear MDPs
claim: Attack effectiveness and cost diverge sharply between vulnerable and intrinsically robust instances: attacks succeed cheaply on one but fail or cost far more on the other.
layout: 2x2 grid of line plots, columns vulnerable vs robust, shared legend per panel
description: A 2x2 grid of line plots, with captions (a) Vulnerable (ε* > 0) under the left column and (b) Robust (ε* ≤ 0) under the right. The top row plots policy difference against episode, and the bottom row plots cumulative poisoning against episode, up to 20000 episodes. Each panel has three curves: orange Black Box, dashed green White Box and blue Baseline. In the vulnerable column, the policy difference of the Black Box and White Box attacks falls to near zero, and cumulative poisoning flattens at about 1.0–1.5 million. In the robust column, the policy difference stays high (about 5000–10000), especially for Black Box, and cumulative poisoning keeps rising to about 2.4 million. The eye goes first to the top-left plot with its sharp orange drop, then compares it with the right column.
caption: Average policy difference (top row) and cumulative perturbations (bottom row) per episode for vulnerable ([ref]) or robust ([ref]) "Half-Cheetah" environments against LSVI-UCB.
abstract: We study reward poisoning attacks in reinforcement learning (RL), where an adversary manipulates rewards within constrained budgets to force the target RL agent to adopt a policy that aligns with the attacker's objectives. Prior works on reward poisoning mainly focused on sufficient conditions to design a successful attacker, while only a few studies discussed the infeasibility of targeted attacks. This paper provides the first precise necessity and sufficiency characterization of the attackability of a linear MDP under reward poisoning attacks. Our characterization draws a bright line between the vulnerable RL instances, and the intrinsically robust ones which cannot be attacked without large costs even running vanilla non-robust RL algorithms. Our theory extends beyond linear MDPs -- by approximating deep RL environments as linear MDPs, we show that our theoretical framework effectively distinguishes the attackability and efficiently attacks the vulnerable ones, demonstrating both the theoretical and practical significance of our characterization.
